text: You've now written a Money class with its own arithmetic. But what if you need that same weighted-average logic for doubles, for integer share counts, and for a custom decimal type — without writing it three separate times? Templates let you write a function or class exactly once, parameterized over a type, and have the compiler generate a correct version for every type you actually use.

A function template is a blueprint. Here, weightedAverage is written in terms of a placeholder type T, and when you call it with two doubles, the compiler deduces T equals double entirely on its own — you almost never have to spell the type out explicitly at the call site.

Function templates parameterize one function; class templates parameterize an entire type, which is exactly how something like std::vector is built under the hood. A class template can also take a non-type parameter — a compile-time constant rather than a type — which is how you fix an array's size at compile time with zero runtime overhead.

FixedBuffer here takes both a type T and a size N. Critically, FixedBuffer of double and 1024 and FixedBuffer of int and 64 are two completely separate compiled types, generated independently — that's why templates cost nothing at runtime, but can grow your binary if you instantiate many combinations.

Before C++20, a template misused with the wrong type produced a dense error buried deep inside the function body. Concepts fix that by letting you name the constraint up front — here, a concept called Numeric — and attach it directly to the template parameter. Call the function with a type that doesn't satisfy it, and the compiler now rejects it immediately with a clear, readable message.

Templates generate a correct, type-specific version of your code for every type you use, at zero runtime cost, and C++20 concepts make both the template's intent and its error messages far clearer.
